title: Efficient Cayley-Hamilton Reduction for Sparse Matrices: The Open Question
content: The header frames the computational question: can the Cayley-Hamilton reduction aeval A p = aeval A (p %ₘ charpoly A) be made efficient for sparse matrices? The answer is yes for three structured types: (1) upper triangular — charpoly = ∏(X - Mᵢᵢ), O(n) from diagonal; (2) block triangular — charpoly = product of block charpolys, divide-and-conquer; (3) strictly upper triangular (nilpotent) — charpoly = Xⁿ, trivial reduction basis. The file extends CayleyHamiltonOQ01 (minpoly reduction) and CayleyHamiltonOQ02 (general charpoly reduction). The key insight: for dense matrices, charpoly requires O(n³); for these sparse structures, it drops to O(n) or O(n·k/k²).
mathContext: The **Cayley-Hamilton theorem**: $p(A) = 0$ where $p = \text{charpoly}(A)$. The **reduction principle**: $f(A) = (f \mod p)(A)$ — polynomial evaluation reduces modulo charpoly. The computational question: computing $p = \text{charpoly}(A)$ for general $A$ requires $O(n^3)$ (Gaussian elimination on $xI - A$). For sparse/structured $A$, can we compute $p$ faster? Yes: upper triangular → $O(n)$; block triangular with $k$ blocks → $O(k \cdot (n/k)^3) = O(n^3/k^2)$.

title: Upper Triangular: Charpoly = ∏(X - Mᵢᵢ) and Efficient Reduction
content: matrix_charpoly_monic wraps Matrix.charpoly_monic — the characteristic polynomial of any square matrix is monic (coefficient of X^n is 1). upper_tri_charpoly_eq_prod: for M.BlockTriangular id (the identity ordering makes upper triangular the standard notion), M.charpoly = ∏ᵢ (X - C (M i i)). Proved by Matrix.charpoly_of_upperTriangular. upper_tri_aeval_eq_aeval_mod: aeval M f = aeval M (f %ₘ M.charpoly) for upper triangular M. Proof: Polynomial.modByMonic_add_div gives f = (f %ₘ charpoly) + (f /ₘ charpoly)·charpoly; applying aeval M and using aeval_self_charpoly = 0 collapses the second term.
mathContext: For upper triangular $M$, $\text{charpoly}(M) = \det(xI - M) = \prod_i (x - M_{ii})$ since $xI - M$ is also upper triangular with diagonal entries $x - M_{ii}$, and the determinant of an upper triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal. **In Lean**: `Matrix.BlockTriangular id M` means $i < j \Rightarrow M\,j\,i = 0$ (upper triangular with the identity block ordering). The modular arithmetic proof uses: $f = q \cdot p + r$ (Euclidean division), so $f(A) = q(A) \cdot p(A) + r(A) = 0 + r(A)$.

title: Power Reduction and Degree Bound for Upper Triangular Matrices
content: upper_tri_power_reduction: M^k = aeval M (X^k %ₘ M.charpoly) for upper triangular M. Proved by applying upper_tri_aeval_eq_aeval_mod to X^k, then simp [map_pow, aeval_X] to convert aeval M (X^k) = M^k. upper_tri_reduction_degree_lt: for Nontrivial R, (f %ₘ M.charpoly).natDegree < Fintype.card n. Proof uses Polynomial.natDegree_lt_natDegree (f %ₘ p ≠ 0 and degree modByMonic < degree p), then Matrix.charpoly_natDegree_eq_dim (charpoly has degree = dimension). Together these say: every matrix power M^k reduces to a polynomial in M of degree < n — exactly n-1 matrix multiplications suffice to evaluate any polynomial.
mathContext: **Cayley-Hamilton corollary**: any $f(A)$ equals $(f \mod \text{charpoly})(A)$ where $\deg(f \mod \text{charpoly}) < n$. So $\{I, A, A^2, \ldots, A^{n-1}\}$ spans the matrix algebra generated by $A$ (as a vector space over $R$). **Matrix.charpoly_natDegree_eq_dim**: $\deg(\text{charpoly}(M)) = n$ where $M$ is $n \times n$. **Nontrivial R hypothesis**: needed to ensure $f \mod p \neq 0$ is well-behaved (degree is undefined for 0).

title: Block Triangular: Charpoly Factors as Product of Block Charpolys
content: block_tri_charpoly_eq_prod: for M.BlockTriangular b (block ordering b : n → α), M.charpoly = ∏ₐ (M.toSquareBlock b a).charpoly. Proved by h.charpoly (the BlockTriangular instance method). block_lower_tri_charpoly: (fromBlocks M₁₁ 0 M₂₁ M₂₂).charpoly = M₁₁.charpoly * M₂₂.charpoly, proved by Matrix.charpoly_fromBlocks_zero₁₂. block_upper_tri_charpoly: symmetric via charpoly_fromBlocks_zero₂₁. block_diag_charpoly: (fromBlocks A 0 0 B).charpoly = A.charpoly * B.charpoly (diagonal blocks). The computational significance: k blocks of size n/k give k · O((n/k)³) = O(n³/k²) for charpoly, compared to O(n³) for the full matrix.
mathContext: **Block triangular charpoly**: for $M = \begin{pmatrix} M_{11} & * \\ 0 & M_{22} \end{pmatrix}$, $\chi_M(x) = \chi_{M_{11}}(x) \cdot \chi_{M_{22}}(x)$. Proof: $xI - M = \begin{pmatrix} xI - M_{11} & * \\ 0 & xI - M_{22} \end{pmatrix}$, and $\det$ of a block triangular matrix is the product of block determinants. **BlockTriangular b**: generalization where blocks are labeled by $b: n \to \alpha$ — the $(i,j)$ entry is zero when $b(j) < b(i)$.

title: Nilpotent Case: Zero Diagonal Forces charpoly = Xⁿ and M^n = 0
content: strictly_upper_tri_charpoly: for M upper triangular (BlockTriangular id) with ∀ i, M i i = 0 (zero diagonal), M.charpoly = X^(Fintype.card n). Proof: apply upper_tri_charpoly_eq_prod, then each factor X - C(M i i) = X (by hdiag i and simp), then Finset.prod_const + Finset.card_univ. strictly_upper_tri_nilpotent: M^(Fintype.card n) = 0 via aeval_self_charpoly and rewriting with the charpoly = X^n result, then map_pow and aeval_X. strictly_upper_tri_pow_vanish: M^k = 0 for k ≥ n, proved by Nat.exists_eq_add_of_le (k = n + d) and pow_add + zero_mul.
mathContext: **Nilpotent matrix**: $M^k = 0$ for some $k$. For strictly upper triangular $n \times n$ matrices (zero diagonal, zeros on and below diagonal), $M^n = 0$ exactly. The characteristic polynomial is $x^n$ (since all eigenvalues are 0). **Cayley-Hamilton gives nilpotency**: $\chi_M(M) = M^n = 0$. The reduction basis for polynomials in $M$ is $\{I, M, M^2, \ldots, M^{n-1}\}$ — only $n$ powers (instead of the generic $n$ powers for non-nilpotent matrices, but now many are 0). **prod_const**: $\prod_{i \in S} c = c^{|S|}$.

title: Diagonal Matrices: O(n) Polynomial Evaluation via Entry-Wise Computation
content: diagonal_pow_off_diagonal: for D with D i j = 0 when i ≠ j (diagonal matrix), (D^k) i j = 0 for i ≠ j. Proved by induction on k: base case uses simp [hij] (identity has 1 on diagonal); inductive step splits the matrix product sum by cases hxj (x = j or not) using hD and ih. diagonal_pow_diagonal: (D^k) i i = (D i i)^k. Proved by induction, using Finset.sum_eq_single i to isolate the diagonal term. These results enable O(n) polynomial evaluation: f(D) is diagonal with f(D i i) on the diagonal, requiring n independent scalar evaluations instead of matrix multiplications.
mathContext: For diagonal $D = \text{diag}(d_1, \ldots, d_n)$: $D^k = \text{diag}(d_1^k, \ldots, d_n^k)$ and $f(D) = \text{diag}(f(d_1), \ldots, f(d_n))$ for any polynomial $f$. **Computational advantage**: evaluating $f(D)$ requires $n$ scalar polynomial evaluations, each $O(\deg f)$ — total $O(n \cdot \deg f)$ vs. $O(n^2 \cdot \deg f)$ for general upper triangular via the reduction theorem. **Finset.sum_eq_single**: $\sum_{x \in S} f(x) = f(i)$ when all other terms are 0.

title: Summary: Four Structured Sparse Cases Answer the Open Question
content: The summary block consolidates the answer to the open question: Cayley-Hamilton reduction CAN be made computationally efficient for four structured sparse matrix types. The four cited results are: upper_tri_charpoly_eq_prod (O(n) charpoly from diagonal), block_tri_charpoly_eq_prod and block_lower_tri_charpoly (divide-and-conquer), strictly_upper_tri_nilpotent + pow_vanish (reduction basis bounded by nilpotency), diagonal_pow_diagonal (direct entry-wise evaluation). The positive results are conditional on the matrix having the respective sparse structure — for dense matrices without structure, O(n³) charpoly computation remains necessary.
mathContext: **Summary of complexities**: (1) Upper triangular: $O(n)$ charpoly — just read diagonal. (2) Block triangular ($k$ blocks size $n/k$): $O(n^3/k^2)$ — factor over blocks. (3) Nilpotent ($M^n=0$): reduction basis is $\{I, M, \ldots, M^{n-1}\}$ — but many are 0. (4) Diagonal: $O(n \cdot \deg f)$ — entry-wise. **Generalization question** (open): can these results extend to approximately sparse matrices (e.g., $\varepsilon$-sparse in spectral norm) or to numerical algorithms with floating-point arithmetic?
